name: Senné

names.when: official from 1904; in printed gazetteers 1907 to 1913

role: One of the two family villages. Seat of the Roman Catholic parish and of the Vécsey estate.

facts.text: First recorded in 1263, when the king gave it to Jakov, the county head of Uzhhorod.
At least 25 serf households in 1427. In 1599: 26 serf houses, a nobles' manor, a church and a rectory.
Down to 5 taxed households in 1715 and 11 in 1720, with some nobles resident. 120 houses and 833 people in 1828.
171 houses and 839 people in 1940.
About 720 people today, on 18.75 square kilometres at 100 metres above sea level.
Part of the Pavlovce nad Uhom estate; the Vécsey family held land here from the 18th to the 20th century.

Urbarial table: Baron István Vécsey had 20 villein households, 3 cottars with a house and 2 without; Count János Barkóczy 1 and 1; Ádám Szirmay 4 and 2; the widow of László Turánszky 1. That is 26 villein households in all.
Roman Catholic church of the Visitation of the Virgin Mary, built in 1718 on the walls of the Gothic church recorded in the 14th century. In 1734 it was brick, newly repaired, with three altars.

The manor house began as a curia of the Dobó family in the 16th century and took its present late-Renaissance form in the first half of the 17th. It later served the Vécsey and Sztáray families as a farm seat and hunting lodge.
Roman Catholic school: a parish school with a teacher by 1774, 61 pupils in 1864, 54 in 1916. No Greek Catholic or Reformed school is recorded here.
Many people emigrated between 1870 and 1890.
A second wave left between 1910 and 1930, mostly for the United States; many came back to buy land.
Baron László Vécsey (1866-1924) ran an estate of about 2,400 cadastral hold from Ungszenna. After 1920 it lay in Czechoslovakia and came under the land reform; his nephew Mihály Sztáray inherited it.
The estate's parcels were sold to villagers after 1921 at several times the official price. Young farms took mortgages and were hit by the 1929 slump.
Four Jewish families were deported in 1942. Soviet troops entered on 27 November 1944.

The name comes from the Slavic word for hay. Matej Bel, in the first half of the 18th century, described the village where the marshy Čierna voda meets the Uh, with fertile fields, fish caught in flood hollows and pigs fed on acorns.
In the Nagykapos district of Ung county until 1920, with the rank of small commune. Its neighbour Iňačovce was in the Szobránc district.
Renamed Ungszenna in 1904, when the law of 1898 gave every settlement in Hungary one unique official name. There were other Szennas in Nógrád and Somogy counties.
About 1588: 23 serf households, of which 10 were peasant farms, 9 cottars and 4 craftsmen, besides the servants of the Dobó curia.

Owners in order, by the municipal history: the crown until 1263; Jakab of Pányok and his heirs to the mid-14th century; the lords of Pavlovce; the Dobó of Ruská in the 16th century; the Vécsey family from the 18th, with the Pethő family holding a part about 1740. Hungarian Wikipedia puts the Csápy family after the Vécseys, the municipal history before.

A parish is recorded by 1322; the municipal history cites mentions of 1317 and 1319. The villagers turned Protestant after 1550. The church was handed back and the Roman Catholic parish refounded in 1718; until then Catholic services were held in the Vécsey manor.

Later history of the church: a tower begun in 1808 collapsed and a new west tower was built with Baron Vécsey's help; lightning burned the roof in 1909, after which the building was lengthened and vaulted; reconsecrated on 15 September 1946 after war damage. State monument register no. 11 243/1.

Parish priests on the published list: Martin Majerčík 1782-1824, Martin Rehák 1824-27, Jozef Spiegel 1828-31, Štefan Rácz 1831-41, Jozef Harkel 1841-50, Juraj Balázs 1850-86, Štefan Rusnák 1886-92, Július Buzinkay 1892-1906, Ján Barna 1906-30, Jozef Biloveský (administrator) 1930-50.

Filials of the Roman Catholic parish changed over time. About 1799: Solymos and both Szeretvas. 1804: Palín, Stretava, Stretavka, Iňačovce, Rebrín, Kráska, Jastrabie. 1917: Jastrabie, Stretavka, Kráska, Stretava, Palín, Rebrín, with Iňačovce missing from the list. Today: Iňačovce, Jastrabie, Palín, Zemplínska Široká.
In 1808 the parish counted 489 Roman Catholics in Senné and 903 in its filials.

By Fényes's gazetteer of 1851: a Slovak, Rusyn and Hungarian village with 580 Roman Catholics, 238 Greek Catholics, 2 Lutherans, 3 Reformed and 22 Jews; a parish church, Baron Vécsey's manor, and a water mill.
In 1904: 484 Roman Catholics, 231 Greek Catholics, 2 Lutherans, 11 Reformed and 26 Jews, 754 people in all.
The Greek Catholics of Senné belonged to the Iňačovce parish. Its chronicle counts 245 of them in Senné, in figures that look interwar. Senné is still a filial of Iňačovce today.
A church school stood opposite the church until 1930, when a communal school replaced it. The manor housed the school after 1946.
The border protocol of 4 April 1939 ran the new Slovak-Hungarian line along the boundary between the fields of Senné and those of Bežovce. Senné stayed on the Slovak side.
Fishing from dugout boats lasted into the 20th century, and geese were kept in flocks of thousands until 1975.
Bishop Ágoston Roskoványi was born here in December 1807. The Hungarian biographical lexicons give the 7th, the Catholic lexicon the 6th.
An entry of December 1861 in the Iňačovce Greek Catholic book gives the residence as Szenna. That is the direct evidence that Senné's Greek Catholics were entered there (PL-H-001).

The archive's catalogue lists the Roman Catholic volumes as nos. 1089 to 1093, on microfilm 287-288: births 1866-1912, marriages 1863-1886 and 1887-1926, deaths 1831-1886 and 1887-1925. It gives the parish district as Senné, Iňačovce, Jastrabie pri Michalovciach, Krášok, Palín, Rebrín, Stretava and Stretavka. No volume of births before 1866 is in that collection.

name: Iňačovce

names.when: 1302, by the Beliana encyclopedia; the Hungarian official form to 1918

role: The other family village. Seat of the Greek Catholic parish, with a Reformed congregation beside it.

facts.text: First recorded in a charter of King Sigismund in 1417. At least 19 serf households in 1427 and 32 serf houses in 1599.
Emptied in the 17th and early 18th centuries: 8 households in 1715, 11 in 1720.
Refilled after 1720 by settlers from the north of Ung and Zemplín counties, Belá nad Cirochou among the places named.
119 houses and 1,023 people in 1828, more than Senné. Close to 200 fewer by 1900. 190 houses and 747 people in 1940. About 900 today.
Owners: the Sztáray family early on; nobles of Pavlovce and Ruská in the 15th to 17th centuries; Count Barkóczy, Baron Vécsey and Szirmay in the early 18th; Thuránszky and Török in the 19th.
Urbarial table: Baron István Vécsey had 29 villein households, 9 cottars with a house and 8 without; Ferenc Kovács 1 and 2; Sándor Szirmay 5, 1 and 1. That is 35 villein households in all.
A Greek Catholic parish from the middle of the 18th century. The 1734 visitation already found the Greek Catholics with their own parish here, and noted that Rusyn was spoken in it.
The first known church was wooden, shingle-roofed, with one bell, dedicated to the Dormition. The present brick church is early 19th century.
The Reformed built a daughter church in 1912. Roman Catholics went to Senné, Lutherans to Pozdišovce, and the Jewish families came under the rabbinate at Senné.
Two schools before 1918. Greek Catholic: 69 pupils in 1864, 79 in 1916. Reformed: 14 pupils in 1864, 41 in 1916.
A salt find is mentioned at the end of the 18th century, and the village had wide meadows.
The Senné fishponds reserve lies in its fields: declared in 1955, 213 hectares, a Ramsar wetland since 1990.
In the Szobránc district of Ung county under Hungary, while Senné was in the Nagykapos district.

The Greek Catholic parish house was built in 1811 and the register has been kept since then. The parish district counted 305 faithful in Iňačovce, 254 in Jastrabie, 245 in Senné and 135 in Stretava, in figures that look interwar.
In the mid-18th century the Greek Catholic parish had Jastrabie, Rebrín, Senné, Stretava and Stretavka as filials.
Lightning on 6 July 1929 and a fire on 1 April 1930 badly damaged the Greek Catholic church archive.
The Reformed of Iňačovce were a filial of the mother church at Lúčky from 1747, and their register was kept there.
The protocol of 4 April 1939 ran the border along the boundaries between Iňačovce and Blatná Polianka and between Iňačovce and Blatné Remety. Iňačovce stayed on the Slovak side.
Sources disagree on the first mention: 1302 in the Beliana encyclopedia, 1417 on the municipal site and elsewhere.
The Greek Catholic church of the Dormition was built about 1800 on the site of the mid-18th-century wooden one. Beliana dates the Reformed church to 1921; the village plan says 1912.
The Greek Catholic register is at the Prešov state archive from 1811. No volume later than 1898 is listed there.

A state birth registration of August 1906 for a child born at Solymos is headed as done at Alsókánya, which is Jastrabie pri Michalovciach. So the civil registrar for Solymos sat at Jastrabie then. The heading is a probable reading by the Demko agent.
Entries cut from the parish book give residences as 'Solymos', 'Szenna' and 'Jesztreb' with house numbers, and name the officiant in 1889 as György Lescsisin, Greek Catholic pastor of Solymos.

The archive's catalogue lists four Greek Catholic volumes, nos. 380 to 383, on film 88: 1811-1831 in Latin; 1831-1859 in Church Slavonic, Latin and Hungarian; births 1861-1870 with marriages and deaths 1861-1874, in Latin; and births 1870-1898 with marriages and deaths 1860-1898. Each holds births, marriages and deaths, so the parish's burials to 1898 are there. Births of 1860 are in none of the four as listed.
The catalogue gives the parish district as Iňačovce, Jastrabie pri Michalovciach, Senné and Stretava.

The 58 strips from this book held by the Duska agent bear the catalogue out. Residences are Solymos, Jesztreb, Szenna, Nagy Szeretva and Kis Szeretva. The language is Latin in 1814-1816, Hungarian in 1837-1848, Cyrillic in 1851-1853, Latin in 1861-1876 and Hungarian from 1877.
Pastors named on the strips: Josef Danilovics in the 1840s and still in 1866; György Lescsisin as assistant in 1885 and as pastor from 1888.

Later hands wrote Slovak notes into the Hungarian-era volumes: a corrected surname on an entry of 1877, and a death of 18 August 1934 on an entry of 1872. So the volume for 1870-1898 was in working use in 1934, after the lightning of 1929 and the fire of 1930.
The Reformed of Iňačovce have a register of their own within the Lúčky parish: births 1819-1927, marriages 1820-1926, deaths 1819-1936 (catalogue no. 592/1).

name: Palín

names.when: Hungarian, as on the parish list for 1917

role: Filial of the Senné Roman Catholic parish in 1734.

facts.text: Listed with Stretava and Stretavka as a Senné filial where Reformed preachers kept the upper hand under the landlord's protection.
A Reformed filial of Stretava in the 1733 list.
The Reformed of Palín had their own register, 1806-1899 (catalogue nos. 787 and 788).

name: Stretava

names.when: Hungarian, as on the parish list for 1917

role: Reformed mother church next door to the Senné parish.

facts.text: A Reformed mother church with a stone church in 1733; its filials were Stretavka, Palín and Kráška.
Counted as a filial of the Senné Roman Catholic parish in the 1734 visitation.

In the Greek Catholic parish district of Iňačovce by the archive's catalogue, and 'Nagy Szeretva' is a residence in an Iňačovce entry of about 1862. The Reformed had their own register here for 1761-1887, covering Stretava and Stretavka (catalogue no. 1173).

name: Stretavka
role: Filial of the Senné parish in 1734, about 1799 and in 1917. Home of the Kulin family, which makes it the likely 'K. Sz.' of the 1838 gift note in the Duska agent's Folder 1.

facts.text: Filial of the Senné Roman Catholic parish in 1734.
A Reformed filial of Stretava in the 1733 list.
In the Nagykapos district of Ung county, like Senné.
Vályi's gazetteer of about 1799 calls both Szeretvas filials of Szenna. Kisszeretva is still on the parish's list for 1917.
The urbarial table lists two Kulin landlords here, Imre and Pál. Fényes names Kulin among the landlords in 1851. The Kulin family of Bánhegyes proved its nobility in Ung county in 1807.

Greek Catholics: sources conflict. The archive's catalogue puts Stretavka in the parish district of Slavkovce (nos. 1099 and 1100, 1805-1895), not of Iňačovce. Yet an entry of about 1871 in the Iňačovce book gives a residence at Kis Szeretva. A Stretavka Greek Catholic may be in either book.

name: Zemplínska Široká

names.when: one of the two villages merged into it
Hungarian, as on the parish list for 1917

role: Rebrín and Kráška were both filials of Senné in 1734.

facts.text: The Senné priest of 1734 gave most of his catechising to Reformed Rebrín.
Iňačovce itself had belonged to the Rebrín parish in the 16th century.

name: Jastrabie pri Michalovciach

names.when: Hungarian, as in the 1939 protocol and the parish list for 1917
as written in Iňačovce Greek Catholic entries of the 1860s to 1891

role: Filial of the Senné Roman Catholic parish in 1733 and 1734.

facts.text: Latin-rite filial of Senné.
On the Slovak side of the April 1939 line, which ran along its boundary with Blatné Remety.
The civil registrar who recorded a Solymos birth in August 1906 signed at Alsókánya, that is here.

House numbers do not stay put. One cottar household of Jesztreb is entered in the Iňačovce book at seven different numbers between 1864 and 1885. Whether the village was renumbered or cottars moved from house to house is not established; a house number alone does not identify a household here.

name: Blatná Polianka
role: Filial of Senné in 1734. Taken by Hungary in March 1939.

facts.text: Filial of the Senné Roman Catholic parish.
Passed to Hungary under the protocol of 4 April 1939; the new border ran along its boundary with Iňačovce.

name: Pavlovce nad Uhom
role: Seat of the estate Senné belonged to, and the Roman Catholic parish for Vysoká nad Uhom.

facts.text: Senné was part of the Pavlovce estate.
A parish of its own in 1734: brick church formerly used by Calvinists, 30 Catholics, more Calvinists and Uniates.
Listed inside the Slovak Michalovce district in 1940.
On the Slovak side of the April 1939 line, which ran along its boundary with Bežovce.
The Roman Catholics of Vysoká nad Uhom belong to this parish. Its register for 1818-1907 is reported filmed, and earlier volumes are placed in the archdiocesan archive at Košice.
Its Greek Catholics were a filial of Čičarovce in 1825.

The catalogue lists its Roman Catholic register as nos. 795 to 798: marriages 1818-1897, births 1869-1896, deaths 1878-1907. Parish district: Pavlovce nad Uhom, Bajany, Čierne Pole, Ťahyňa and Vysoká nad Uhom. Births before 1869 and deaths before 1878 are not in that collection.

name: Veľké Kapušany

names.when: as written in the 1839 circular, Duska Folder 1

role: District seat south of Senné. The clergy meeting of 14 May 1839 in the Duska agent's Folder 1 was held here.

facts.text: Seat of one of the six districts of Ung county in the early 20th century.
Senné was in the Veľké Kapušany district before 1960.
The Hungarian line of March 1939 ended near here, at its south-east corner.

name: Sobrance
role: District seat north-east of the villages. Its whole district went to Hungary in April 1939. Today the Roman Catholic deanery for Senné.

facts.text: Seat of one of the six districts of Ung county.
All 41 villages of the Sobrance district passed to Hungary under the protocol of 4 April 1939.
The Senné parish is in the Sobrance deanery today.
The Senné parish moved from the Michalovce deanery to the Sobrance deanery in July 2012.

name: Michalovce

names.when: a village beside the town, joined to it in 1925; 'Sztrajnyán' is read, with doubt, on a baptism strip of about 1887

role: District town for both villages today. It was in Zemplén county, not Ung, before 1918.

facts.text: Iňačovce has been in the Michalovce district since 1921. Senné was counted in it in 1940 and has been in it for good since 1960.
The present district straddles the old Zemplén and Ung county line.
Nearest railway station to Senné, 17 kilometres away.

Stráňany, now a part of the town, was a separate village until 1925. Its Greek Catholics were in the Michalovce Greek Catholic parish, with Vrbovec, and its Roman Catholics in the Michalovce Roman Catholic parish, with Lastomír, Krásnovce, Močarany, Petrovce nad Laborcom and Topoľany.

Registers at Prešov: Greek Catholic nos. 670 to 675 (1795-1905; 1876-1890 is no. 673), Roman Catholic nos. 661 to 669 (1826-1899; births 1883-1895 are no. 667). Each has a duplicate volume for 1882-1895.
In the mid-18th century the Greek Catholics of the town were served by a cleric from Topoľany.

name: Uzhhorod
role: County town of Ung and seat of the Greek Catholic bishop of Mukachevo. The archive where Maria Demko's birth record is said to be.

facts.text: Capital of Ung county.
Seat of the Mukachevo Greek Catholic eparchy, which the Iňačovce parish belonged to.
Back under Hungarian rule from November 1938, when the First Vienna Award recreated Ung county.
The district library for the Roman Catholic clergy, the subject of four circulars in the Duska agent's Folder 1, was kept here.

name: Prešov
role: State archive holding the church registers of both villages.

facts.text: Holds the Iňačovce registers: Greek Catholic 1811-1898, Reformed 1747-1940, Roman Catholic 1863-1926.
Reported home of the originals of the Senné Roman Catholic register, 1831-1926.

name: Berehove
role: Branch of the Zakarpattia state archive. Holds 1869 census sheets for Ung county.

facts.text: The Ung county 1869 census questionnaires are here. They are not online; the reading room needs advance registration and the director's permission.

name: Košice

names.when: Latin, as in the 1837 circular in Duska Folder 1

role: Seat of both of today's dioceses for the villages: the Roman Catholic archdiocese and the Greek Catholic eparchy.

facts.text: The Senné parish belongs to the Archdiocese of Košice.
The Iňačovce parish belongs to the Greek Catholic diocese of Košice.

name: Satu Mare

names.when: Latin, as the circulars in Duska Folder 1 are dated

role: Roman Catholic bishop's seat for Ung county from 1804. The circulars in the Duska agent's Folder 1 were sent from here.

facts.text: Ung county's Latin-rite parishes passed from Eger to the new diocese of Szatmár in 1804.
The Vécsey family's main seat, the Sárköz estate, was in Szatmár county and went to Romania in 1920.

name: Mukachevo
role: Gives its name to the Greek Catholic eparchy. The bishop sat at Uzhhorod.

facts.text: The eparchy was erected by the Pope in 1771. A reorganisation in 1818 left Ung county inside it.

name: Belá nad Cirochou

names.when: as spelled in the Iňačovce plan

role: Named as one source of the settlers who refilled Iňačovce after 1720.

facts.text: After 1720 many settlers came to Iňačovce from the north of Ung and Zemplín, this village among them.

name: Bežovce
role: Passed to Hungary in April 1939. Its boundary with Senné became the state border.

facts.text: The protocol of 4 April 1939 ran the border along the boundaries of Bežovce with Vysoká nad Uhom, Pavlovce nad Uhom and Senné, leaving Bežovce on the Hungarian side.
Seat of the Greek Catholic deanery that the Čičarovce parish belonged to, and from 1771 to 1806 the Greek Catholic parish for Vysoká nad Uhom. Not in the Slovak state's list for 1940.

name: Vysoká nad Uhom

names.when: 1782 military map; and as written in the baptisms of 1875 to 1883 held by the line agents
Hungarian official name from 1904 by the place-name dictionary; Hungarian Wikipedia says the old name ran to 1899

role: The Viszoka of the baptisms of 1875 to 1883 held by the Duska and Demko agents, house numbers 120, 121 and 132. Its Greek Catholics were registered at Čičarovce, its Roman Catholics at Pavlovce nad Uhom.

facts.text: First recorded in 1214, in a royal charter confirming a grant to the Premonstratensian provostry of Lelesz, which owned the village for centuries.
After the plague of 1709-1710 the tax list of 1715 found 7 peasant households and 1 cottar household.
By Fényes's gazetteer of 1851: a Hungarian, Rusyn and Slovak village with 331 Roman Catholics, 275 Greek Catholics, 182 Reformed and 6 Jews. Landlord: the provost of Lelesz.
In the Nagykapos district of Ung county until 1920, like Senné.
Census counts: 142 houses and 1,106 people in 1880; 1,187 people in 1890; 209 houses and 1,203 people in 1900, with 110 more counted as abroad; 1,175 in 1910; 1,162 in 1921; 1,100 in 1930.
With 142 houses in 1880, a house numbered 132 in 1882 is in range. Ung county had only this one Viszoka.
Greek Catholics: in the early 18th century a handful attended the church at Lekárovce. From 1771 the village was a filial of Bežovce, and from 1806 until the 1940s a filial of Čičarovce.

It became a Greek Catholic parish of its own only in the 1940s: provisionally from 1 March 1945 and formally on 26 September 1948 by the parish history; another local page says 1944. The church of the Nativity of the Mother of God is dated 1892 by the parish and earlier in the century elsewhere.
Roman Catholics: a filial of the Pavlovce nad Uhom parish, in 1733 and still today. No source makes it a Roman Catholic filial of Čičarovce.
Reformed: a filial of Pavlovce until 1721, with a wooden church about 1780 and the present one of 1912; a filial of Stretava since 1931.

1939: the border protocol of 4 April runs the line along its boundaries with Lekárovce and Bežovce, and the Slovak state's list for 1940 has 'Vysoká' in the Michalovce district with 230 houses. So it stayed in Slovakia. The same list shows its population as 0, which looks like a fault in the published table.

Against that: the Senné and Vysoká municipal histories speak of Hungarian troops entering in March 1939, and a census database labels the village as Hungarian-administered in 1941. Read here as an occupation during the fighting that the protocol did not make permanent (PL-H-012).
Liberated on 23 November 1944. Emigration is noted in the 1930s.

The archive's catalogue confirms the Roman Catholic side: Vysoká nad Uhom is in the parish district of Pavlovce nad Uhom (nos. 795 to 798). The Reformed had a register of their own here, 1853-1897 with deaths from 1837, covering Vysoká, Pavlovce and Ťahyňa (nos. 1456 and 1457).

An entry of about 1831 has a Greek Catholic's son of Viszoka baptised by the Latin-rite parish priest of Pálóc, 'with the consent of the local parish priest'. Pálóc is Pavlovce. It shows the two rites' clergy standing in for each other in a cholera year; it does not show cholera in the village.

Reformed seniorate of Michalovce: the congregation

name: Čičarovce

names.when: Hungarian; 'csicseri g.k. lelkész' in the officiant's title on strips of 1875 and 1879

role: Seat of the Greek Catholic parish that served Vysoká nad Uhom from 1806 to the 1940s. The 1882 baptism strip comes from its book (PL-H-009).

facts.text: A village of three mother churches: Roman Catholic, Greek Catholic and Reformed. In 1851 Fényes counted 545 Reformed, 251 Roman Catholics, 175 Greek Catholics and 53 Jews, and called it Hungarian.
155 houses and 1,243 people in 1828. In 1910: 1,203 people, of whom 460 Reformed, 331 Greek Catholic, 327 Roman Catholic and 82 Jewish.

The Greek Catholic parish existed by 1771, under the Mukachevo eparchy, in the Bežovce deanery, with a church of the Protection of the Mother of God. In 1751 the village had still been a filial of Maťovce.
In 1825 the Greek Catholic parish had 12 filials, among them Vysoká nad Uhom, Pavlovce nad Uhom and Vojany, and over 1,500 faithful.

Greek Catholic parish priests: Jozef Kubek 1847-1881, Ján Csurgovics 1882-1886, Andrej Azary 1886-1901, Štefan Dubay 1901-1905, Július Bellovics 1905-1913, Mikuláš Barna 1914-1917, Eugen Kiss from 1918. The Vysoká parish history gives the same sequence.
That list matches the records in hand: strips of 1875 and 1879 are signed by József Kubek as Greek Catholic pastor of Csicser, and a strip of January 1883 by János Csurgovich.

The Roman Catholic parish of St Ladislaus was refounded in 1780, in the Lower Ung deanery of the Szatmár diocese from 1804. Its filials never included Vysoká. Its priest from 1868 to 1890 was András Polányi.
In the Nagykapos district of Ung county until 1920. Ceded to Hungary in November 1938 with Veľké Kapušany and 23 villages of its district, and under Hungary until 1945.
Not in the Slovak state's list of Michalovce district municipalities for 1940.

links.label: Greek Catholic eparchy of Košice: the parish
Prešov state archive: catalogue of church registers

name: Belža

names.form: Kapolnas Belse, Siget Belse, Sándor Belse

role: Seat of the Greek Catholic parish that served Gyňov and Seňa. The baptism copies of 1894 and 1895 belong to its register.

facts.text: A Greek Catholic mother church stood at Sziget-Bölzse by the parish survey of 1774-1782, with Kápolna-Bölzse, Sándor-Bölzse, Gönyű and Szina among its filials. The lists of 1792 and 1806 say the same.
The parish passed from the Mukachevo eparchy to the new eparchy of Prešov about 1818. In the 1890s it was in the Kassa district of that eparchy; the district for 1894 exactly is inferred, not read.
Fényes in 1851: three Rusyn and Slovak villages with 318 Greek Catholics, 139 Roman Catholics, 10 Jews and 5 Reformed. Greek Catholics were 56.9 per cent of the people in 1880.
Borovszky, in the 1890s: 46 houses and 279 Hungarian- and Slovak-speaking inhabitants. He dates the church to 1818; another source says 1808.
Resettled after the plague of the early 18th century with Greek Catholic Rusyns and Roman Catholic Slovaks.
In the Kassa district of Abaúj-Torna county until 1920. Ceded to Hungary in November 1938.
Today the parish has Gyňov and Kechnec as active filials; Seňa and Valaliky are among the inactive ones.

links.label: Greek Catholic eparchy of Košice: Belža parish
Borovszky: Greek Catholic parishes of the Kassa district

name: Gyňov

names.when: Hungarian to 1905; 'Gönyü' in the baptism copies of 1894 and 1895

role: Named as a residence, houses 24 and 2, in the Belža baptism copies. A Greek Catholic filial of Belža.

facts.text: A Greek Catholic filial of the Bölzse mother church in the surveys of 1774-1782, 1792 and 1806, and an active filial of Belža today. That confirms the Duska agent's reading of 'Gönyü' as Gyňov and not the Gönyű on the Danube.
Fényes in 1851: a Slovak and Hungarian village with 170 Roman Catholics, 130 Greek Catholics, 40 Reformed and 15 Jews.
55 houses and 361 people in 1828. Borovszky, in the 1890s: 43 houses and 286 Slovak-speaking inhabitants. House numbers 2 and 24 are in range.
Roman Catholics belonged to the Kassamindszent parish in 1915.
In the Kassa district of Abaúj-Torna county, moved to the Füzér district in 1908. Under Hungary again from 1938 to 1945, by its Hungarian official name in those years.

name: Seňa

names.when: Hungarian; 'Szina' in a baptism copy of about 1894

role: Named as a residence, house 182, in the Belža baptism copies. A Greek Catholic filial of Belža. Not to be confused with Senné.

facts.text: A Greek Catholic filial of the Bölzse mother church from the 1770s, and still listed under Belža today.
Fényes in 1851: a Hungarian, Slovak and Rusyn village on the Pest high road, with 762 Roman Catholics, 397 Reformed, 240 Greek Catholics, 159 Jews and 27 Lutherans.
190 houses and 1,413 people in 1880; 224 houses and 1,546 people in 1900. A house numbered 182 in 1894 is in range.
Sources disagree on the Roman Catholics: a parish restored in 1782 by one account, a filial of Kechnec until 2008 by the Kechnec parish.
Fényes spells this village 'Szinna', one letter from Szenna (Senné) and the same as Szinna (Snina). An index entry under any of the three needs its county checked.
In the Kassa district of Abaúj-Torna county. Ceded to Hungary in November 1938.

name: Valaliky

names.when: Hungarian name of Bernátovce, one of the villages merged into Valaliky in 1961
Hungarian name of Košťany, the third

role: Three candidates for the unidentified '-falva' village of the Belža baptism copies. Not yet decided between them (PL-H-011).

facts.text: Valaliky was formed in 1961 from Všechsvätých, Bernátovce, Buzice and Košťany. It is the only filial of the Belža Greek Catholic parish today that contains villages with Hungarian names ending in -falva.
All three lay in the Kassa district of Abaúj-Torna county and were Roman Catholic filials of Kassamindszent in 1915. Each was small enough, at 33 to 55 houses, to have a house numbered 5.
Not confirmed: that any of the three was a Greek Catholic filial of Bölzse in 1894 and 1895 and not of the Greek Catholic parish in Kassa town.

name: Lastomír

names.when: Hungarian; 'Lasztomér' on a baptism strip of about 1887

role: Named as a residence in a baptism strip of about 1887 held by the Demko agent. In Zemplén county, outside the Iňačovce and Čičarovce parishes.

facts.text: In Zemplén county until 1918, about 6 km south of Michalovce. 137 houses and 1,001 people in 1828. Many emigrated between 1880 and 1910.

Greek Catholics: a register of its own at Prešov, no. 531, with births 1860-1928 and marriages and deaths 1890-1937, and a duplicate for 1891-1895 (no. 532). The parish district is Lastomír alone. A Greek Catholic baptism here in 1887 should be in no. 531.
The Greek Catholic parish of Šamudovce also lists Lastomír in its district (nos. 1213 to 1218, 1786-1928). Before 1860 for births, and before 1890 for marriages and deaths, that is the book to try.
Roman Catholics belonged to the Michalovce parish. The Reformed had a parish here with a wide district that took in Michalovce itself (nos. 533 to 535, 1787-1924).

name: Eger

names.when: Latin, as in the 1839 notice in Duska Folder 1

role: Roman Catholic bishop's seat for Ung county until 1804. Off the map to the south-west.

facts.text: The 1734 visitation of the Senné parish was made for the bishop of Eger.

name: Budapest

Urbarial tables for Szenna and Solymos are published from there.
